Package frc.robot.subsystems.elevator

Class SimElevatorSubsystem

java.lang.Object
edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.elevator.AbstractElevatorSubsystem
frc.robot.subsystems.elevator.SimElevatorSubsystem
All Implemented Interfaces:
edu.wpi.first.util.sendable.Sendable, edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Subsystem, Subsystem, AutoCloseable
public class SimElevatorSubsystem extends AbstractElevatorSubsystem
The elevator implementation used in simulation, test runs, and CI.

This is a sibling of ElevatorSubsystem, not a configuration of it. Both extend AbstractElevatorSubsystem and therefore share the entire public API and control loop, but each supplies its own mechanism: the real one drives motor controllers, this one advances a WPILib ElevatorSim. Nothing in the shared layer knows the difference.

Why a separate class rather than an IO behind the same subsystem. A team reading ElevatorSubsystem should see only the code that runs on their robot; a robot should never ship a physics model. Splitting by class makes that structural instead of a convention, and it means the simulation can own state the real mechanism has no use for — the plant, its step, and its thread — without that leaking into the hardware path. 


 // Robot code picks one once at startup:
 AbstractElevatorSubsystem elevator = RobotBase.isReal()
     ? new ElevatorSubsystem(...)
     : new SimElevatorSubsystem(ElevatorHardware.CONSTANTS);

Why it wraps WPILib's model. ElevatorSim already models a DC motor, a gearbox, a drum, and a gravity load, and it is the model every team's simulation is calibrated against. Reimplementing it would drift from real results and would have to be maintained. Following the physics simulation guide, the closed loop is a WPILib PIDController plus ElevatorFeedforward; only the plumbing between the library's units and WPILib's doubles lives here. The same computation is used by ElevatorSubsystem for real hardware, so simulated and real mechanisms behave alike.

Two ways to run it

Real-time — the default constructor starts a daemon thread that steps the plant every 20 ms, so the mechanism moves by itself exactly as it would on a robot. This is what a full robot simulation wants.

Stepped — SimElevatorSubsystem(ElevatorConstants, boolean) with false leaves time frozen until step(double) is called. This is what tests want: two identical runs then produce bit-identical trajectories, with no wall clock involved, so a suite cannot become flaky.

    • SimElevatorSubsystem

      public SimElevatorSubsystem(ElevatorConstants constants)
      Creates a simulated elevator that advances itself in real time.

      Use this for a full robot simulation, where nothing else is stepping the loop.

      Parameters:
      constants - the physical description of the mechanism

    • SimElevatorSubsystem

      public SimElevatorSubsystem(ElevatorConstants constants, boolean realTime)
      Creates a simulated elevator, choosing whether it advances itself.

      Passing false is what makes a test deterministic: the plant only moves when the test calls step(double).

      Parameters:
      constants - the physical description of the mechanism
      realTime - true to step in the background, false to step on demand

    • holdPosition

      protected void holdPosition(edu.wpi.first.units.measure.Distance position)
      Description copied from class: AbstractElevatorSubsystem
      /** Drives the carriage to hold position.

      Called once per loop while the mechanism is enabled. Implementations close the loop however suits their hardware: a vendor motor controller's onboard position control, or a WPILib PIDController plus feedforward, as ElevatorSubsystem and SimElevatorSubsystem both do.

      position is already clamped to the travel range, so implementations need not re-validate it.

      Specified by:
      holdPosition in class AbstractElevatorSubsystem
      Parameters:
      position - the height to hold, measured from the zero position

    • driveOpenLoop

      protected void driveOpenLoop(double velocityMetersPerSecond)
      Description copied from class: AbstractElevatorSubsystem
      Drives the carriage open-loop at a velocity.

      Not reached from any command in this API; it exists so a subclass can build a homing routine — drive into the lower stop until AbstractElevatorSubsystem.isAtLowerLimit() trips, then AbstractElevatorSubsystem.zeroPosition() — without reaching around the abstraction for raw voltage.

      Specified by:
      driveOpenLoop in class AbstractElevatorSubsystem
      Parameters:
      velocityMetersPerSecond - the velocity to drive at, positive raising the carriage

    • releaseOutput

      protected void releaseOutput()
      Description copied from class: AbstractElevatorSubsystem
      Stops commanding the mechanism.

      Called while idle and on SubsystemBase.stop(). Whether the carriage then holds or sags is the hardware's brake mode, not a decision this method makes.

      Specified by:
      releaseOutput in class AbstractElevatorSubsystem

    • step

      public void step(double dtSeconds)
      Advances the simulated carriage by one robot loop.

      The plant only moves when this is called, which is what makes a stepping test reproducible. Call it after SubsystemBase.periodic(), so the mechanism responds to this loop's command rather than the previous one's.

      Parameters:
      dtSeconds - the timestep to integrate, in seconds

    • isReal

      public boolean isReal()
      Description copied from interface: Subsystem
      Returns whether this mechanism is driving real hardware.

      Callers use this to skip hardware-only work, and tests use it to skip assertions that only make sense against real motors. A simulated implementation returns false.

      Returns:
      true for real hardware, false for a simulated implementation
